inlineContent.text: While an update or a query is running, the world can’t be changed in other ways. To spawn,
despawn or restructure entities from inside one, record the changes in
and
them afterward.
A world is a value, like an array or a dictionary: a copy is independent of the original.
Copying is cheap, because each component type’s storage is shared between copies until one of
them writes to it, and then only that type’s storage is copied. This makes it easy to keep an
earlier state, for undo or for comparing two steps of a simulation:
Despawning an entity makes every copy of its handle
stale
. A world can reuse the slot the
entity occupied, but a stale handle never names the new occupant. Use
to test
whether a handle is still live.
Operations that take an entity trap when it is stale, in the same way an array subscript traps
when its index is out of range. Each has a
spelling that throws instead, for entities
whose liveness you can’t be sure of:
Because a world is a value, a call that reads a world reads it as it was before the call’s
arguments were evaluated. An entity spawned in an argument of a call on the same world, as in
, isn’t in the world the call reads, so the call traps as
though the new entity were stale. Spawn into a constant first, then make the call:
The components of each type are stored in a sparse set: a dense array of components with a
sparse array from entity slot to position. Reading, adding, replacing and removing one
component are O(1), and visiting every component of a type walks contiguous memory.
